claim.cause: employed_days counted every day from the first assignment's start to the last one's end, so gap days between assignment rows (leaving and being rehired) were paid as salaried days with meal allowance, using the row that had already ended.

feedback.approach: I read the salary, allowance, employment and payslip code and saw that only base salary and meal allowance were off. Both depend on the employed days, which made me suspect that employed_days spans from the first assignment's start to the last one's end. I exported the employment_for calls from the trace with pmdb and checked them in Python. That showed rehire gaps in September, and their salary and weekday allowance came to exactly 16,904.43 and 502.50. I fixed employed_days and confirmed the same deltas by re-running the old and new versions on the traced arguments.
feedback.key_step: Exporting the arguments of every employment_for call and finding gaps between assignment rows that fall in September; the salary and weekday allowance for those gap days matched HR's differences exactly.
feedback.wasted_effort: One query failed because pmdb can't compare strings with >, and I had to switch to export plus Python.
pmdb_problems: String ordering comparisons (> and < on ISO date strings) aren't supported, and the documentation doesn't say which operand types each operator accepts.
There's no way to refer to adjacent elements in a list, such as consecutive rows, so gap detection had to move to Python.
pmdb_wishes: Support < and > on strings, or provide date helpers.
Aggregations like sum/group-by over matches, so totals can be compared with the report without exporting.
Sorting and zip or pairwise list helpers in conditions.
other_wishes: A small anonymized sample export, to test a full re-run end to end.

claim.cause: The re-send fingerprint left out the scheme's network_ref, so separate transit clearings with no auth code and a date-only time (same card, merchant and fare) were treated as processor re-sends and dropped, which lost €808.30 of clearings on 202 cards.

feedback.approach: I compared call counts from `show functions` (on_clearing 4144 vs post_clearing 3955), then read consumer.py, dedup.py and parking.py alongside the log. Because 'dropped 421 processor re-sends' looked suspicious, I exported every classify call with pmdb and, in Python, compared each 'resend' with the first message that had the same fingerprint. That showed 284 clearings whose only difference was network_ref. Summing the re-sends whose network_ref had not been seen before gave exactly €808.30 over 202 cards.
feedback.key_step: Diffing each message classified as 'resend' against its original with the same fingerprint: the only field that differed was network_ref, on transit clearings that had no auth_code and a date-only transaction_time.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first sum compared against only the first message with each fingerprint and got 820.90, so I needed a second pass keyed on network_refs already seen. I also printed a long `show $1` of fingerprint calls, which added nothing.
pmdb_problems: `show $N` has no limit option, so I had to pipe it through head to keep the output manageable.
Comparing one call with another (re-send vs. original) can't be done in the query language, so I exported to JSONL and wrote Python for it.
pmdb_wishes: A `show $N limit K` option, or a count-by/group-by aggregate (e.g. group resends by event_type).
A way to join or correlate two observations in a query, e.g. find an earlier call with an equal fingerprint and diff the arguments.
Sum or other aggregate functions over the matches, so the €808.30 check could stay inside pmdb.
other_wishes: A sample of the raw queue messages, or a schema for the clearing payload, documenting which fields stay stable across processor re-sends.

claim.cause: The duplicate-detection identity (IDENTITY_FIELDS used by fingerprint) left out network_ref, so a second or later presentment of the same authorization for the same amount (e.g. split shipments) was classified as a processor re-send and dropped instead of posted.

feedback.approach: I started with `show functions` and saw that on_clearing had more calls than post_clearing (4144 vs 3955). The log said 421 processor re-sends were dropped, so I read dedup.py, consumer.py and parking.py. Then I exported every classify call to JSONL and used Python to compare each clearing marked as a re-send with the first message that had the same fingerprint. 284 of them differed only in network_ref, they were on 202 cards, and the distinct ones summed to exactly €808.30.
feedback.key_step: Exporting the classify calls and diffing each 'resend' clearing against the first message with the same fingerprint. This showed that only network_ref differed, on 202 cards, for €808.30.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first try ran `show $0` on 9k fingerprint calls, and the output overflowed into a persisted file I never read. My first sum came to €820.90 because it counted repeated network_refs more than once, so I needed one more pass to get €808.30.
pmdb_problems: `show $N` on a large selection prints everything with no limit or paging, which flooded the output.
Nothing in the query language lets you correlate two different calls (for example, joining a resend with the earlier call that has the same key), so I had to export and do it in Python.
The docs don't say whether `select` queries can access nested fields of opaque objects such as NamedTuple messages. It turned out they are tables, but I only learned that from the export.
pmdb_wishes: A `show $N limit K` option, or a count/group-by aggregate (for example, group by r).
Joins or self-correlation between selections, for example 'calls in $1 whose argument field equals one in $0'.
A built-in diff of two observed argument values.
other_wishes: A small sample of raw queue message bodies or a fixture to replay the job end to end, so I could check the fix against the full pipeline and not just the dedup step.

claim.cause: employed_days counted every day between a person's first and last assignment row, including days in gaps between rows, so segment_at paid the previous ended row's salary and meal allowance for days with no contract.

feedback.approach: I read the salary, allowance, absence and employment code and the log. Because both base salary and meal allowance were too high, I suspected the set of days being paid. I exported every base_salary call from the trace to JSONL and checked in Python whether each paid day was covered by an assignment row. That turned up 9 people with gaps between rows, and the gap days added up exactly to the €16,904.43 and €502.50 differences.
feedback.key_step: Exporting the base_salary calls with pmdb and checking each paid day against the assignment rows' valid_from/valid_to. This showed paid days that fell between two rows, e.g. P10085's row ending 2026-09-20 with the next starting 2026-10-01.
feedback.wasted_effort: I first tried to query base_salary calls where the unpaid set was non-empty, but a set is an opaque object in pmdb, so the query failed. I also briefly checked the absence kinds, which didn't help. A small Python replay crashed once because of that same opaque set.
pmdb_problems: Python sets are recorded as opaque objects ({"$object": null} in the export), so I couldn't query or export the unpaid-days argument; `u.len()` failed with 'value of type object is not a table'.
`show` on large result sets produces huge output with no built-in limit or field projection, so I had to pipe it through head/awk.
The error message doesn't say which expression or variable caused the type error.
pmdb_wishes: Record sets and frozensets as arrays.
A `limit N` clause, or `show $N limit N`.
Projection: show only selected bound variables or fields instead of the whole call line.
Aggregations such as sum/group-by over bound variables (e.g. total returned value per cost centre).
other_wishes: A sanitized or synthetic HR export so the whole job could be re-run end to end and the totals compared with HR's preview.
A per-person breakdown of HR's preview, to diff payslips directly.

claim.cause: The function was including days that fall in gaps between employee assignments where valid_to of one assignment ends before valid_from of the next assignment begins.

feedback.approach: Used pmdb to query segment_at function calls and found many returning segments for dates after their valid_to end dates. Exported the results to JSON and analyzed them to identify 9 employees with gaps in their assignment dates that were being incorrectly included in payroll calculations.
feedback.key_step: Exporting segment_at observations to JSON and discovering that 98 days across 9 employees had day > segment.valid_to, which directly explained the €16,904.43 salary discrepancy when divided by average salaries.
feedback.wasted_effort: Initial exploration of round_half_up and other payroll functions before narrowing down to the employment/days logic. Also briefly considered if segment_at itself needed fixing before recognizing employed_days was the root cause.
pmdb_problems: Query syntax for comparing fields wasn't supported (had to export to JSON to analyze segment.valid_to vs day)
No pipe operator support—had to use export to analyze large result sets
Output size made it hard to explore interactively without exporting
Documentation lacked examples of complex queries involving multiple field comparisons

Pipe operators to filter/process output without exporting
Built-in aggregation or grouping functions
More example queries in documentation showing real debugging scenarios

Documentation or comments in employed_days clarifying the assumption that assignments don't have gaps
A data validation check in employment_for to flag gaps in assignments

claim.cause: The dedup fingerprint lacked a per-transaction reference, so distinct offline clearings (no auth_code, day-only transaction_time) at the same merchant/card/amount/day collided and later ones were wrongly dropped as processor re-sends.

feedback.approach: I read the ledger source to understand the posting pipeline (holds, parking, dedup) and noticed dedup.py's fingerprint used card/amount/currency/transaction_time/auth_code without any transaction-level reference. I used pmdb to list all classify() calls for clearing messages, exported them to JSON Lines, and grouped them by that fingerprint in a Python script to look for groups containing more than one distinct network_ref — which would mean distinct transactions being misclassified as resends. This found exactly 213 colliding groups affecting 202 cards, matching the bank's exception report count, and showed the collisions were all offline transactions (no auth_code) with date-only transaction_time.
feedback.key_step: Exporting the classify() calls to JSON and grouping by the dedup fingerprint to find groups with multiple distinct network_ref values — that proved the fingerprint was conflating genuinely different transactions, not just catching real resends.
feedback.wasted_effort: An early side-quest trying to reconcile the exact €808.30 / 202-card figures down to the cent cost some time (I got €820.90) without changing the diagnosis or fix; it was useful for confidence but not strictly necessary to find or fix the bug.
pmdb_problems: The `show functions` output doesn't distinguish call sites, so I couldn't tell from that alone that classify() was called once per message in the main loop versus elsewhere; had to read source to confirm.

No built-in way to group/aggregate matches (e.g. count distinct values of a field across matches) inside pmdb itself, so I had to export to JSON Lines and post-process in Python for the key analysis (grouping by fingerprint, finding collisions).

Large `show $N` outputs get truncated to a file with only a preview shown, which is fine but means a large `select` followed by `show` is often a wasted round-trip once you realize you should have exported instead.
pmdb_wishes: A `group by` or aggregate query capability (e.g. count distinct values of an expression across the matches of a select) so collision-finding like this wouldn't require exporting and writing a separate script.
Ability to filter/select based on a derived key shared across multiple calls (e.g. 'calls that share the same value of expr X but differ in value of expr Y') directly in the query language.
other_wishes: A way to diff two conceptual runs (e.g., simulate the fix against the recorded trace and get a direct before/after totals comparison) rather than hand-rolling that in a Python script.

claim.cause: The re-send fingerprint omitted the presentment's network_ref, so distinct offline clearings sharing card/amount/merchant and a time-of-day-less transaction_time (e.g. repeated same-amount transit taps) collided and later ones were wrongly dropped as duplicates.

feedback.approach: I read the ledger code (consumer.py, dedup.py, parking.py, holds.py) to understand the posting pipeline and noticed dedup.py's fingerprint-based re-send detection relied on fields (card, amount, currency, transaction_time, auth_code) that could collide for offline clearings lacking auth_code and with date-only transaction_time. I used pmdb to export all classify() calls for clearing-type messages, then cross-referenced network_ref across same-fingerprint groups in a Python script to prove distinct transactions were being misclassified as resends and dropped.
feedback.key_step: Exporting all clearing classify() calls via pmdb and grouping by the dedup fingerprint to find groups with multiple distinct network_ref values — that pinpointed the exact collision and, once I summed the wrongly-dropped amounts, it matched the reported €808.30 across 202 cards exactly.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first narrower analysis (only resend-classified messages, checking for differing network_ref within that subset) undercounted the missing amount/cards (342/51 vs the true 808.30/202) because it didn't correctly account for which ref among a collision group was the one actually posted as NEW; I had to redo the analysis comparing NEW refs vs RESEND refs properly.
pmdb_problems: No way to directly express 'group by' or aggregate within a query, so cross-referencing fingerprints/network_refs required exporting to JSONL and post-processing in Python
show $N on a large result set produced a very long single-line-per-call dump that got truncated/saved to a side file rather than shown inline, slightly breaking flow
pmdb_wishes: A lightweight way to group/count matches by a derived key (e.g. 'select ... group by t.field') to spot collisions without round-tripping through export+Python
Ability to join two queries/variables (e.g. correlate classify() NEW results with classify() RESEND results by a shared key) directly in the query language
other_wishes: A way to replay/validate a fix against the recorded trace directly within pmdb (e.g. 're-run function with patched code against recorded args') instead of manually reconstructing Message objects and reset state in a separate script
Direct access to the actual queue dump (even partial) would have let me do a true end-to-end re-run instead of a manual replay simulation

feedback.approach: I used pmdb to extract all booked refunds and analyzed them by status. I discovered NovaPay had 103 pending refunds that other providers (Kestrel, Lumen) didn't have, totaling €4,658.96. I cross-referenced this with the €5,027.67 discrepancy to identify the root cause: pending refunds were being counted alongside succeeded ones due to having different event IDs.
feedback.key_step: Exporting booked refunds grouped by status and comparing the status distribution across providers. Kestrel and Lumen had only succeeded refunds; NovaPay had both pending and succeeded. This pattern across providers revealed pending refunds were anomalous and shouldn't be counted.
feedback.wasted_effort: I spent substantial time searching for an exact match for the remaining €83.07 discrepancy after my main fix, investigating disputes, orphan refunds, and fees—all unproductive detours. My fix addresses ~94% of the issue but may not be 100% complete.

No direct support for aggregations (SUM, COUNT); had to export and post-process with Python

claim.cause: NovaPay sends a separate event for each status change of a refund, and the ledger booked every non-failed one (pending, repeated succeeded, and ones that later failed) as another refund instead of counting each refund once in its latest, succeeded state, which overstated NovaPay refunds by €5,027.67.

feedback.approach: I read the NovaPay adapter and the ledger, then used pmdb to export every NovaPay Ledger.apply_refund call and grouped them in Python by refund ref and status. That showed pending events booked alongside their later succeeded events, some succeeded events repeated, and some refunds that later failed. I exported every NovaPay refund event, including the ignored ones, and confirmed that keeping each refund's final state and booking only succeeded ones gives exactly 11,938.78. Then I fixed Ledger.apply/apply_refund and replayed all traced transactions through the fixed ledger.
feedback.key_step: Exporting the NovaPay apply_refund calls and grouping them by ref: the same ref showed up as pending, then succeeded (sometimes twice), with each event booked; later, the final-state-per-ref sum matched the statement to the cent.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first hypothesis was that pending refunds alone explained it. That sum (4,658.96) didn't match, so I needed a second pass to find the duplicate-succeeded and later-failed cases. Before grouping by ref I also skimmed money.py, which was a dead end.
pmdb_problems: Named-tuple arguments appear as tables in exports, but the docs don't say whether Txn fields can be used directly in conditions (t.provider). It worked, but I had to guess.
Each invocation loses its variables, so every new question meant re-running a select and re-exporting.
Nothing in pmdb does aggregation or group-by, so I had to round-trip through JSONL and Python for every sum or count.
pmdb_wishes: Built-in aggregations such as sum, count, and group-by over a field (e.g. sum t.settle_amount group by t.ref, t.status)
Shorthand for selecting on a field of an object argument without binding the whole thing
Ability to export directly to stdout to avoid temp files
Persistent variables across invocations or an interactive session mode
other_wishes: A sample of anonymized raw NovaPay refund events, or provider docs describing the refund status lifecycle
The August trace/report for comparison, to see why it reconciled (probably no refund updates that month)

claim.cause: NovaPay sends a new event each time a refund's status changes, and the ledger added every non-failed refund event (pending, repeated succeeded) to refunds and never reversed refunds that later failed, so each refund should count once, by its latest status.

feedback.approach: I read the ledger, the NovaPay adapter, the loader and the log. I saw that 421 NovaPay refunds were received but only 410 booked, so I pulled every NovaPay Ledger.apply_refund call from the trace and grouped them by status and refund ref in Python. That showed pending refunds booked next to their later succeeded event, a few refunds with two succeeded events, and refunds that went succeeded → failed without being reversed; together these account for exactly €5,027.67. I patched the ledger to book each refund once, by its latest succeeded state, then replayed all exported Ledger.apply calls through the patched ledger to confirm the statement figures.
feedback.key_step: Grouping the traced apply_refund arguments by ref and status: 103 'pending' refund events had been booked, many of them sharing a ref with a 'succeeded' event. Then checking the skipped failed refunds against earlier succeeded events of the same ref closed the last €83.07.
feedback.wasted_effort: A little: my first try at 'counted once per unique ref' gave a figure that didn't match. That pointed me to the failed-after-succeeded case, so it wasn't entirely wasted.
pmdb_problems: show output prints NamedTuples as {k: v} text with no quoting, so I had to regex-parse it in Python; commas inside values would break that parsing. Using export to JSONL fixed this, but I only switched to it later.
Nothing in the docs says whether named tuples keep field order in show output, or whether opaque objects (Book) can be inspected at all, e.g. their attributes.
pmdb_wishes: Aggregations in the query language (group by a field, sum, count), e.g. sum t.settle_amount grouped by t.status, so I wouldn't need a Python post-processing step.
A way to show only selected fields or expressions (show $0 select t.ref, t.status), so long Txn reprs don't fill the output.
Inspecting the state of opaque objects (e.g. Book.refunds) at call entry and exit.
other_wishes: A small anonymized sample of the export, or NovaPay's documentation of the refund lifecycle (statuses and how often it redelivers an object with a new event ID), would have confirmed the semantics without inferring them from the data.

feedback.approach: I read the payroll modules (salaried.py, employment.py) to understand proration logic, then used pmdb to dump every base_salary call from the trace and inspected employments with multiple assignment segments. Checking segment_at calls against their matched segment's valid_to revealed cases where a day fell after the segment's valid_to but before the next segment's valid_from (a gap), and the function silently returned the stale expired segment. I then reconstructed corrected pay for the 9 affected employees in Python and the recomputed overpayment summed to exactly €16,904.43 (base) and €502.50 (meal allowance), matching the reported discrepancies to the cent.
feedback.key_step: Querying all segment_at(segments, day) -> result calls via pmdb and filtering for cases where day > result.valid_to, which directly exposed the stale-segment fallback for gap days.
feedback.wasted_effort: Two early pmdb invocations where I exported the wrong variable ($0 instead of the just-created $1) because `select` always creates the 'next' variable rather than overwriting $0 in a fresh session — cost a couple of redundant commands but was quickly caught by checking line counts.
pmdb_problems: `select` numbering ($0, $1, ...) increments per invocation of the pmdb process in a way that's easy to misremember when issuing multiple `select`/`export` pairs in one heredoc — I twice exported the wrong variable by habit from assuming $0 meant 'the last select'.

Arguments that are non-trivial Python objects (e.g. a `set` for `unpaid` days) are exported as opaque `{"$object": null}` placeholders with no identifying info, so correlating them with other calls required relying on call order rather than being able to query their contents directly.
pmdb_wishes: A way to give opaque objects a stable id (e.g. object identity hash) in the export so separate observations referencing 'the same' runtime object can be correlated without relying on call ordering.

A condition/query form to filter on a field of the returned record against a field of an argument directly (e.g. `where r.valid_to != none && day > r.valid_to`) worked fine here, but a quick way to also pull the *next* or *previous* call on the same arguments (e.g. 'calls to f adjacent in time for the same object') would have shortened the gap-detection query.
other_wishes: Having the actual HR export (even a synthetic/anonymized fixture with the same shape) would have let me re-run the full pipeline end-to-end to confirm the fix against real output instead of only reconciling against the trace and a hand-built synthetic test.

claim.cause: NovaPay resends refund status updates (pending/succeeded/failed) for the same refund under new event ids, and the ledger booked each as an independent movement instead of superseding the previous state for that object, double-counting settled refunds and counting still-pending ones as paid out (fixed together with adding "pending" to config/settings.toml's ignored_statuses).

feedback.approach: I first read the provider adapters and ledger code to understand the booking model, then used pmdb to export all booked refund transactions and grouped them by refund object id (ref). This revealed that NovaPay refunds had duplicate refs with different event ids and transitioning statuses (pending -> succeeded -> sometimes failed), which the loader's event-id-based deduplication didn't catch. I then brute-force-tested several aggregation hypotheses against the exact target numbers NovaPay's statement gave until one (keep only the latest-by-timestamp state per ref, counting only if its final status is 'succeeded') matched exactly, then verified the combined fix (unbook-on-supersede in Ledger.apply + adding 'pending' to ignored_statuses) reproduced the target to the cent by replaying the full trace through the real code.
feedback.key_step: Exporting all Ledger.apply_refund calls via pmdb and grouping NovaPay's booked refunds by their object id (ref) revealed dozens of groups with the same ref appearing under different event ids with different statuses (pending/succeeded/failed) — proof that the same economic event was being booked more than once.
feedback.wasted_effort: A long stretch of manually guessing subset-sum predicates (pending-only, duplicate-succeeded-only, various combinations) to match the exact target diff of 502767 cents before realizing two separate fixes (unbook-on-supersede AND adding 'pending' to ignored_statuses) were both needed together; this trial-and-error with Python scripts in /tmp took much longer than directly reconstructing the Txn stream and testing against the real Ledger code from the start.
pmdb_problems: The `self` parameter requirement in call patterns wasn't obvious at first (e.g. `Ledger.apply_refund(book, txn)` fails silently with a warning instead of an error, requiring a second attempt with `(self, book, txn)`)

No way to directly query/join on nested dict/table fields across two different function's recorded calls in one query (e.g. correlating a refund's `ref` with its parent charge amount required exporting both and joining in Python rather than in pmdb itself)
No built-in groupby/aggregate query capability, so any 'find duplicates by field X' analysis had to be exported to JSONL and post-processed externally
pmdb_wishes: A groupby/aggregate query mode (e.g. 'group calls by argument field and show counts/sums') would have let me find the duplicate-ref pattern in one query instead of exporting and writing ad hoc Python
Support for joining across two selections (e.g. matching a refund's parent to a charge's ref) directly in the query language
Clearer error/warning when a call pattern's arity doesn't match due to a missed `self`, ideally suggesting the correct arity
other_wishes: A way to actually re-run the job against the real export (or a sanitized/synthetic subset) rather than having to reconstruct a synthetic export purely from trace data to validate the fix end-to-end

Inline documentation or a comment in novapay.py mentioning that refund status can transition (pending -> succeeded/failed) with new event ids per notification, which would have pointed directly at the bug instead of requiring trace-driven discovery

claim.cause: The hold state was not checked before posting clearings; clearings with non-open holds should be parked instead of posted to prevent incorrect accounting.

feedback.approach: I examined the code structure and message flow using pmdb to count function calls and compare parsed vs handled messages. I analyzed the on_clearing function's logic for handling clearings with and without holds. I hypothesized that the function was missing a check for hold state, causing clearings to be posted even when their holds were in CLEARED or REVERSED states rather than OPEN.
feedback.key_step: Recognizing that on_clearing checked if a hold exists (is not None) but did not check if the hold is in the correct 'open' state. When a hold is CLEARED (after a final clearing is posted), subsequent clearings should be parked as late presentments, not posted immediately.
feedback.wasted_effort: Extensive circular analysis of the code logic, trying to determine if post_clearing() was being called correctly and exploring fee calculation and to_minor() functions. claim.cause: Deduplication fingerprint used merchant's transaction amount instead of programme currency billing amount, causing resent clearings with FX rate changes to be incorrectly skipped.

feedback.approach: I used pmdb to trace function calls and calculate totals of parked/posted clearings, then compared these to the missing amount. After extensive analysis of the on_clearing and hold logic failed to explain the discrepancy, I reasoned through FX rate scenarios and realized the dedup fingerprint was using the merchant's transaction amount instead of the programme currency billing amount.
feedback.key_step: Recognizing that when clearings are resubmitted due to network timeouts after FX rate changes, the merchant's amount field stays identical but billing_amount differs. Since the fingerprint used amount, these were incorrectly deduplicated and skipped rather than posted as distinct settlement amounts.
feedback.wasted_effort: Extensive time (~2 hours) tracing through on_clearing, holds.consume, post_clearing, and parking logic trying to find why clearings weren't being posted. This was misdirected since the root cause was clearings not being processed at all due to dedup, not clearings being processed incorrectly.
pmdb_problems: Query syntax for filtering was unintuitive (unclear which operations were supported)
No straightforward way to trace a specific message object through multiple calls
Large result sets overwhelming - had to export to JSON to make sense of them
Hard to correlate which parked messages became released messages without manual tracking

Filter by message data fields (e.g., show post_clearing where billing_amount > 100)

SQL-like query interface for familiarity
other_wishes: Static code analyzer that could flag mismatched IDENTITY_FIELDS vs actual message fields
Unit tests exercising the FX rate / dedup scenario
Ability to run the fixed code against the trace to verify the fix

Enhanced logging showing which dedup classifications occurred and why

claim.cause: NovaPay sends separate pending/succeeded/failed events (new event_id each time) for one refund as it settles, and the ledger booked every event instead of only the latest per object, while 'pending' (not yet actually paid out) wasn't excluded from booking at all, overstating refunds by €5,027.67.

feedback.approach: I compared the report to NovaPay's statement and noted only refunds were off by a fixed amount. Using pmdb, I pulled every booked NovaPay refund transaction from the trace and found that 83 refund object IDs appeared multiple times with different statuses (pending, then succeeded or failed), each as a separate event with its own event_id. I then brute-force tested hypotheses (exclude pending, dedupe by latest event per ref, or both) against the trace data until a combined rule reproduced NovaPay's exact stated refund total to the cent.
feedback.key_step: Exporting all novapay refund 'normalize' calls from the trace and grouping them by the refund object id (ref), which revealed that ~20% of refund objects fired multiple events (pending/succeeded/failed) with distinct event_ids that the loader's event_id-based dedup couldn't catch.
feedback.wasted_effort: Several rounds of hand-computing candidate totals (succeeded-only, latest-wins, pending-excluded, etc.) against the target figure before landing on the exact combination (latest-event-wins AND exclude pending) that matched NovaPay's number to the cent.
pmdb_problems: Argument pattern matching requires exact arity including self, so f(x, y) silently fails to match f(self, x, y) with only a warning after the fact rather than a clearer upfront hint in the query syntax itself.

export/show output nests positional args as a list, and self/book objects print as opaque '<...object at 0x...>' strings, requiring a second pass in Python to pull out the actual dict fields of interest.
pmdb_wishes: A query primitive to group/aggregate matches by a derived key (e.g. group-by on an argument field) so I wouldn't have to export to JSONL and re-implement grouping/summing in Python.

Ability to reconstruct or replay a generator's yielded sequence directly (e.g. for read_raw_events) rather than only call-level argument/return snapshots, to avoid needing a workaround via normalize() calls.
other_wishes: A way to run the actual job against a small synthetic export without having to hand-craft provider JSON payloads from reading the provider adapter source.
Direct access to (or a sanitized sample of) the real export file would have let me validate end-to-end instead of reconstructing the pipeline from trace exports.

claim.cause: employed_days only checked the overall employment start/end, not each assignment row's valid_to, so gaps between assignment rows (e.g. a break in service) were counted as employed and segment_at then paid the stale previous row for those gap days.

feedback.approach: I started by reading the salaried.py and allowances.py source to understand the proration/allowance formulas, then used pmdb to export call traces (base_salary, meal_allowance, absence_days, unpaid_days, hourly_pay) to JSONL and reimplemented the formulas in Python to check self-consistency against the actual trace data. When that showed the functions were internally correct, I searched for a structural pattern distinguishing affected vs. unaffected cost centres, which led me to check each person's assignment rows for gaps between segments. Quantifying those gaps and simulating a fix (excluding gap days from employed_days) reproduced HR's numbers to the cent, confirming the root cause.
feedback.key_step: Computing, for every person, the gaps between consecutive assignment rows (previous.valid_to vs next.valid_from) and finding that the total weekday gap-days in September was exactly 67 (502.50/7.50) and the salaried gap-days exactly accounted for the 16,904.43 base salary excess.
feedback.wasted_effort: A long stretch testing alternative hypotheses (mid-month raise proration variants, part-time weekly-hours proration, holiday handling, sick/vacation precedence, hourly-worked-days-only allowance) before considering employment gaps; these were reasonable but unproductive since the self-consistency checks had already shown the functions matched their own formulas exactly, which should have pointed me toward 'the bug is in what data reaches the function' sooner.
pmdb_problems: Values of non-JSON-serializable types (e.g. the `unpaid` set argument) are exported as opaque `{"$object": null}` placeholders with no identifying info, which made cross-referencing calls by argument value impossible and forced me to reconstruct those sets from a different function's trace instead

No way to join/correlate rows across two exported traces other than assuming call order alignment (no call id or parent/child linkage in the exported JSON), which is fragile when a function is called from multiple sites
I had to export to JSONL and post-process in Python for any nontrivial aggregation (sums, group-by cost centre) since the query language itself has no aggregation beyond count
pmdb_wishes: Preserve a stable per-call identifier (and ideally the enclosing call's identifier) in exports so traces of different functions from the same logical invocation can be joined reliably
Represent opaque objects (sets, custom classes) with at least a repr or sorted element list when they're simple containers, instead of collapsing them to null
Built-in aggregation in the query language itself (sum/group-by over a field) so simple 'is this consistent' checks don't require exporting and writing a separate script
other_wishes: A way to run the actual pipeline end-to-end on synthetic/redacted data (even a tiny fabricated HR export) to verify the fix numerically against the real code path, rather than only validating via a hand-rolled reimplementation of the formulas
Some indication in the trace or logs of 'employment gaps' or similar data-quality signals, since this is exactly the kind of silent edge case that's easy to miss without an explicit invariant check
